The ajaeng is a Korean zither-type chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 312.22. The body is broad and flat and carries twisted silk strings, traditionally seven or eight, sometimes nine to twelve. The player sits on the floor, lays the instrument on a grass mat (chosang) and draws a thin forsythia stick across the strings like a bow, and may also pluck them. It mainly takes the bass in an ensemble, and its timbre is close to the cello's but rougher. The ajaeng is used in Korean court, aristocratic and folk music, and also appears in contemporary classical music and film scores.
牙箏源自中國 yazheng，高麗時期傳入韓國。1430年，負責整理宮廷音樂與典: The ajaeng comes from the Chinese yazheng and reached Korea in the Goryeo period. In 1430 the office responsible for court music and ceremonies brought the ajaeng into the playing of Tang music, and records from the reign of Sejong also describe its form. Early on the ajaeng was used only for Tang music, and by the reign of Seongjong it was also used for hyangak. Traditionally it was divided into the large ajaeng, used for jeongak, and the small ajaeng, used for sanjo and folk music. From the second half of the twentieth century improved ajaengs appeared, extending the range.
